after.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,xz,\,z+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})+0-(z+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-z}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{{x}^{2}-z}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,z-2x⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=3.$  Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
after.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,z-2x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,2y⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2(3-x)+2(x+y)-2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(6-2x+2x+2y-2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,-3y,\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x-y+2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*
content.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y+2$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=2,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-2.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y+2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,-3y,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x,\,-3y,\,x-y+2⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x+3y-(x-y+2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(4y-2)\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}(4y-2)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4y-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(4y-2)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}(4y-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[x]_{0}^{3}\cdot {[2{y}^{2}-2y]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 12 \\  & =36\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,z,\,2x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨y,\,3,\,2x-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(2x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}(-(2x-y))\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[({x}^{2}-xy){|}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,]\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(3-y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[3y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
